text: Build versus buy -- a real framework for AI components. Every ADR in the last lesson's example implicitly answered a build-vs-buy question. This lesson makes that decision explicit and gives it a real framework, because 'buy is always cheaper' and 'build is always more flexible' are both unreliable defaults.

Here's the concrete decision: Northbeam's RAG pipeline needs a re-ranking step, re-ordering retrieved documents by relevance before they reach the LLM. The team can build this in-house, or buy it as a managed API. A decision made on vibes instead of real numbers is exactly the kind of thing a written ADR and a good architecture review will catch.

Run the build numbers. Assume a fully-loaded engineer cost of fifteen thousand dollars a month: three months to build and test, plus half a month per quarter of ongoing maintenance. That's forty-five thousand dollars to build, sixty thousand over two years of upkeep -- a total build cost of a hundred and five thousand dollars over two years.

Now the buy side. At Northbeam's two million daily requests, with thirty percent needing re-ranking at an illustrative three hundredths of a cent per call, that's a hundred and eighty dollars a day -- a hundred thirty-one thousand four hundred dollars over two years. In this specific scenario, building is actually about twenty-six thousand four hundred dollars cheaper than buying -- the opposite of the common assumption.

But cost alone isn't the whole decision. Speed to market favors buying -- three months of build time is three months the feature isn't shipped. Team expertise matters -- if the team's never built a re-ranker before, the real timeline likely runs longer, with real quality risk. Vendor risk cuts the other way, introducing a dependency that can raise prices or disappear. And differentiation matters: a genuine competitive advantage is worth owning; a commodity capability is better bought.

So the framework is three steps. Run the real cost numbers over the actual relevant time horizon, typically two to three years, not just the initial cost. Name the non-cost factors explicitly -- speed, expertise, vendor risk, and differentiator-versus-commodity. And write the decision down as an ADR, including which factor actually tipped it -- because 'we decided to build it' with no reasoning is exactly the underspecified decision this chapter is teaching you to avoid.

Even with a real cost advantage, build versus buy can still go the other way once those other factors are weighed. Next up: weighing trade-offs across cost, latency, quality, and maintainability -- what to do when there are three options, not two, and nothing wins on every axis.
